readerTitle: Your cleaning company built an app. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (상업 청소 회사가 만든 업무 도구, 소매 기업 내부 운영팀의 대시보드) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 업무용 도구 출시는 기능을 알리는 일이 아니라, 첫 고객, 그들이 느끼는 고통에 맞춘 메시지, 거래 크기에 맞는 판매 방식을 하나로 맞추는 일이다.
misconception: 좋은 도구를 만들었으면 최대한 넓게 알리고 기능을 설명하면 저절로 팔린다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 (MKT-08-01 첫 고객 고르기, MKT-08-02 메시지-시장 적합성, MKT-08-05 영업 주도 vs 셀프서브)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 관리자 1명당 월 $20 × 관리자 3명 = 월 $60, 월 $60 × 12개월 = 연 $720.
관련 레슨은 MKT-08-01과 MKT-08-05로 지정했습니다. 4번 카드는 MKT-08-02(메시지-시장 적합성)도 함께 사용합니다. 관련 레슨이 두 개로 제한되어 있어 목록에는 넣지 않았습니다. 편집 시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your cleaning company built an app. Now what?
body: Maya runs a commercial cleaning company with 40 cleaners. Two years ago she built a simple photo checklist app. Supervisors snap each finished room, and clients see proof the same night.
Complaints dropped. Then other cleaning company owners started asking if they could use it too. Maya decides to launch it as a product. Her first three choices will decide whether it sells.

image.label: A cleaner photographing a tidy office room with a phone
image.brief: 밤의 사무실. 청소 직원이 정돈된 회의실을 휴대폰으로 찍고, 화면에 체크 표시가 뜬다. 따뜻하고 차분한 일러스트. 실제 브랜드 로고나 앱 화면 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who should Maya sell to first?
body: She has a working tool, little money and no sales team. Three options are on the table.

options.text: Run online ads to every cleaning company in the country
options.feedback: Wide reach, but she'd pay to reach people who don't feel the pain yet. She'd learn slowly and spend fast.

options.text: The five owners who already asked, all cleaning offices like hers
options.feedback: **Who to sell to first** at work: start where the pain is sharpest and access is easiest. These buyers already want it and will tell her what's missing.

options.text: A large facility firm with thousands of cleaners
options.feedback: One deal could be huge. But big buyers bring long approvals and feature demands that would pull a tiny team off course.

cards.title: Three said yes. Two didn't.
body: Maya offered the app to all five owners. Three signed up within a week. Two tried it and stopped.

The difference wasn't the app. The three clean offices where clients complain and threaten to cancel contracts. Photo proof saves them arguments. The two clean homes, where the owner is often there to check the work.
Her first customers had taught her who the tool was really for: cleaning firms whose clients are *never in the room*.

cards.title: What should the website headline say?
body: Maya now knows her best buyers: office cleaning firms tired of client complaints. Which headline should go on the sign-up page?

options.feedback: Accurate, but it describes the feature, not the problem. Buyers have to work out on their own why they'd care.

options.text: "Show clients every room is done, before they complain"
options.feedback: **Message-market fit** at work: the words match the exact pain of the chosen segment, so the right buyer recognizes themselves in seconds.
It sounds bigger, but it speaks to no one in particular. Office cleaning owners may not see their problem in it.

cards.title: Let the size of the deal pick the sales method.
body: Maya charges $20 per supervisor a month. A typical customer has three supervisors. Each deal is small, and the owner decides alone.
That points to **self-serve**: sign up online, a free trial, and a short setup call. A salesperson chasing $720 deals would cost more than they bring in. This is **sales-led vs self-serve** at work.

breakdown.label: Per customer, per year
breakdown.detail: Too small to pay for a sales team

cards.softwareNote: Many software tools follow the same rule: small, quick decisions suit self-serve sign-up, while large deals with many approvers need a salesperson to guide them.

cards.title: Your first customers are kinder than the market.
body: The first three owners knew Maya. They forgave bugs, called her directly and set up the app with her help.
Strangers won't. When she moves beyond people she knows, the setup must work without her, and the headline must persuade without a friendly phone call behind it.
Early wins show the idea works for a small, warm group. They don't yet prove it works for everyone in that segment.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a retailer.
body: An operations team at a regional retail chain built a dashboard that flags products about to run out. They want all 12 regional managers to use it. Nobody has to.

options.text: Email all 12 managers a link and a launch memo
options.feedback: That's self-serve for a tool that needs explaining. Most busy managers will open it once and go back to their old spreadsheets.

options.text: Start with the two managers who lose most sales to empty shelves, meet them weekly, then share their results
options.feedback: **Who to sell to first** plus a hands-on, **sales-led** approach. Two strong success stories will persuade the other ten better than a memo.

options.text: Ask the CEO to make it required for everyone
options.feedback: You'd get logins quickly. But forced use often stays shallow, and you lose the honest feedback that would make the tool better.

cards.softwareNote: Internal tools face the same launch problem as outside products. Colleagues choose whether to adopt them, so they need the right first users and the right amount of help.

cards.title: A launch is three choices that have to agree.
body: You used three ideas from this unit: **who to sell to first**, **message-market fit**, and **sales-led vs self-serve**. Pick the buyers who feel the pain most. Describe that pain in their words. Then sell in a way the deal size can pay for.
**Try it today:** for one product, write your first buyer, your headline and your sales method on one line. Check that each one fits the other two.
